headline: Wall Street posts its third consecutive losing session as benchmark crude oil surges past $101 a barrel, magnifying stubborn inflation anxieties and shifting Federal Reserve interest rate parameters. U.S. stock indices tumbled deep into the red on Wednesday as intensifying geopolitical clashes between the U.S. and Iran stoked strict fears of a prolonged regional energy blockade. Compounding the equity pressure, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield spiked to its highest tier since 2023 at 4.83% after a long-dated government debt buyback layout disappointed market expectations. This double-barrel yield and energy surge caused investors to sharply adjust positions ahead of key inflation data, with traders now pricing in a 60% probability of an upcoming Fed rate hike.

Wall Street posts noticeable declines to kick off the holiday-shortened week as a sharp crude oil spike and expanding international trade barriers rattle market sentiment. U.S. benchmark indexes fell on Tuesday as investors processed escalating Middle East energy blockades and the implementation of massive cross-border tariffs. A supply shock pushed Brent crude futures up toward the $100 per barrel threshold, immediately reviving fears of structural core inflation and solidifying expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike later this month. Risk premiums expanded across the board, pulling high-beta tech hardware and consumer cyclical groups onto the defensive.

Wall Street edges lower as a hotter-than-expected August jobs report triggers an immediate surge in Federal Reserve interest rate hike expectations. U.S. stocks finished the week on a soft note on Friday after the Labor Department reported that nonfarm payrolls surged by 162,000 in August, wildly overshooting consensus economic estimates [U.S. stocks finished the week on a soft note on Friday]. This dramatic evidence of labor market strength instantly caused traders to price in over a 50% chance of an upcoming Fed rate hike, pushing short-term two-year Treasury yields up to 4.37% and triggering institutional rotation out of credit-sensitive and retail sectors [U.S. stocks finished the week on a soft note on Friday].
